title: Lost Spring
summary: In two linked sketches, Anees Jung describes children whose childhood is stolen by poverty: Saheb, a ragpicker in Seemapuri on the edge of Delhi, and Mukesh, a boy from a bangle-making family in Firozabad. The piece exposes the exploitation of child labour and the vicious circle of poverty, tradition and apathy that keeps families trapped.

notes.heading: About the author
notes.html: Anees Jung (born 1944) is an Indian journalist and writer who has worked as editor and columnist for leading newspapers. The chapter is drawn from her book Lost Spring: Stories of Stolen Childhood, which records the lives of underprivileged children across India.

notes.heading: Gist
notes.html: Part one follows Saheb-e-Alam, whose family fled floods in Dhaka and now scavenges garbage in Seemapuri. He dreams vaguely of school and later works at a tea stall, earning money but losing his freedom. Part two visits Firozabad, where generations of families work in dark, hot glass furnaces making bangles, losing their eyesight. Mukesh dares to dream of becoming a motor mechanic, while the elders accept their fate as a family destiny.

notes.heading: Detailed summary
notes.html:
Saheb in Seemapuri. The author meets Saheb every morning scrounging for gold in the garbage dumps of her neighbourhood. His family came from the green fields of Dhaka, Bangladesh, which storms had repeatedly swept away. Asked why he does not go to school, he says there is none nearby and he would go if one were built. When the author half-jokingly offers to start a school, he takes her seriously, which embarrasses her because she had made a promise she could not keep.

His name means ‘lord of the universe’, an irony given his barefoot poverty. Many ragpickers go barefoot, and they explain it as tradition rather than poverty. The author recalls a boy whose wish for shoes is part of a long-unfulfilled dream. Seemapuri, on the periphery of Delhi, houses about 10,000 ragpickers in structures of mud and tin, without sewage or running water. Their ration cards let them vote and buy grain. For adults garbage means survival; for children it is wrapped in wonder, since one might find a coin or even a rupee.

Later Saheb is seen holding a steel canister, working at a tea stall for 800 rupees and meals. But the canister seems heavier than the light plastic bag he used to carry, because now he is no longer his own master.

Mukesh in Firozabad. Firozabad is the centre of India’s glass-blowing industry, where about 20,000 children work near furnaces of high temperature, often losing their eyesight before they become adults. Mukesh’s family lives in a stinking lane. His grandmother has watched her husband go blind from the dust of polishing bangles. She says it is their karam, their destiny. A young bride, Savita, solders glass pieces mechanically, unaware of the sanctity of the bangles she makes. The family cannot organise: they are caught between moneylenders, middlemen, police, officials and politicians, and anyone who tries to unite is beaten and jailed.

Yet Mukesh insists he will be a motor mechanic and will learn to drive a car. The author notes that his dream looms like a mirage among the dust of the town, but it is a dream nonetheless.

notes.heading: Themes
notes.html:
• Lost childhood: spring, the season of growth, is stolen from children forced into labour.
  • Child labour and exploitation: illegal work in hazardous industries, ignored by law enforcers.
  • The vicious circle of poverty: lack of education, debt and middlemen keep families trapped for generations.
  • Fatalism versus hope: elders accept suffering as fate, while Mukesh shows that dreams can break the cycle.
  • Apathy of society: broken promises, as the author’s own unfulfilled offer of a school shows.

notes.heading: Character sketches
notes.html:
Saheb-e-Alam: a cheerful, innocent ragpicker with a grand name and no means. He is curious and eager to learn but lacks opportunity. His shift to the tea stall shows how money comes at the cost of freedom and childhood.

Mukesh: a bangle-maker’s son who refuses to accept the family trade as destiny. Determined and independent, he wants to become a motor mechanic even if the garage is far away. He represents hope.

The grandmother: represents the older generation’s fatalistic acceptance of the family’s ‘god-given lineage’.

notes.heading: Title justification
notes.html: Spring is the season of freshness and growth, a metaphor for childhood. The children in the chapter never enjoy this season of life; they are pushed into labour, poverty and dangerous work. Their spring is ‘lost’, making the title both poetic and accurate.

notes.heading: Message and values
notes.html: Education and awareness are the only way out of the cycle of poverty. Society and government must enforce laws against child labour, and individuals must not make empty promises. The chapter also values courage to dream, as seen in Mukesh.

keyTerms.definition: A settlement on the periphery of Delhi where migrant ragpickers live in mud-and-tin homes.
Town in Uttar Pradesh famous for glass and bangle making, where children work near hot furnaces.
Destiny or fate decided by one’s deeds; the grandmother uses it to explain blindness and poverty.
A condition that continues from generation to generation without relief.
Moneylenders who keep poor bangle-makers in debt.
An illusion of water in a desert; used to describe Mukesh’s dream glimmering in dusty Firozabad.
Saheb-e-Alam means ‘lord of the universe’, yet he owns nothing and walks barefoot.
‘Spring’ stands for childhood in the title.

mcqs.q: Where had Saheb’s family originally come from?
mcqs.explanation: Saheb’s family left Dhaka after storms repeatedly destroyed their fields and homes.
It means lord of the universe, ironic for a barefoot ragpicker.

mcqs.q: Why was the author embarrassed after offering to start a school?
options: She did not know how to teach.
Saheb took her half-joking promise seriously and she could not keep it.
mcqs.explanation: Saheb came back asking if the school was ready; she had made a promise she never meant to keep.

mcqs.q: For the children of Seemapuri, garbage is:
options: wrapped in wonder, since they may find a coin
mcqs.explanation: For adults it means survival, but for children garbage holds wonder; a coin or rupee might turn up.

mcqs.q: Why did Saheb feel the steel canister was heavier than his plastic bag?
options: It was made of heavy steel.
He had lost his freedom and was now a servant.
mcqs.explanation: The plastic bag was his own; the canister belonged to the tea-stall owner. The weight is the loss of freedom.

mcqs.q: What is the main hazard faced by children in Firozabad’s bangle industry?
options: Losing their eyesight in dark, hot furnaces
mcqs.explanation: Working near high-temperature furnaces in dim light causes many to go blind early.

mcqs.q: How does Mukesh differ from his family?
options: He wants to become a bangle trader.
He dreams of becoming a motor mechanic.
He wants to be a policeman.
mcqs.explanation: Unlike the fatalistic elders, Mukesh insists he will be a motor mechanic.

mcqs.q: Which of these is NOT part of the vicious circle described in Firozabad?
mcqs.explanation: The circle consists of moneylenders, middlemen, policemen, bureaucrats and politicians; teachers are not mentioned.

mcqs.q: The grandmother attributes her husband’s blindness to:
mcqs.explanation: She calls it the family’s karam, showing fatalistic acceptance.

options: a young girl soldering glass pieces, unaware of what bangles signify
mcqs.explanation: Savita works mechanically on bangles, unaware of their sanctity as symbols of a married woman.

questions.q:
Read the situation and answer: The author notes that many ragpickers walk barefoot and explain it as an old tradition, but she sees it differently.
(a) What reason do the ragpickers give? (1)
(b) What does the author think is the real reason? (1)
(c) Name the tone of the author here. (1)
(d) What does this show about how the poor cope? (1)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) They say walking barefoot is a tradition.

(b) She believes it is a way of hiding their perpetual poverty.

(c) Ironic and sympathetic.

(d) It shows that the poor sometimes dignify their deprivation as custom in order to bear it.

questions.q: What does garbage mean to the adults and children of Seemapuri?
questions.answerHtml: For adults, garbage is a means of survival; it gives them their daily bread and a roof over their heads. For children it is wrapped in wonder, because while sifting through it they might suddenly find a coin or a rupee.

questions.q: Why does the author call Mukesh’s dream a ‘mirage’?
questions.answerHtml: A mirage is an illusion that seems real but recedes. Mukesh’s wish to be a motor mechanic shines like a bright possibility, but in dusty, poor Firozabad, with no money or training, it seems hard to reach. Still, it is a hopeful dream.

questions.q: Why can’t the bangle-makers of Firozabad organise themselves into a cooperative?
questions.answerHtml: They are trapped in a web of sahukars, middlemen, policemen, bureaucrats and politicians. Years of exploitation have made them fearful and fatalistic. Anyone who tries to unite them is hauled up by the police and beaten, so they lack leadership and courage.

questions.q: ‘Lost Spring’ explains the grinding poverty and traditions which condemn thousands of children to a life of exploitation. Explain. (120–150 words)
questions.answerHtml:
Anees Jung shows how poverty and tradition together rob children of their spring. In Seemapuri, Saheb and other children of migrants spend their mornings scavenging garbage instead of going to school. Their families, displaced by floods, live without water or sanitation and see ragpicking as the only way to survive. When Saheb gets a job at a tea stall, he earns 800 rupees but loses his freedom.

In Firozabad, tradition is the chain. Families have made bangles for generations, and children work near furnaces that destroy their eyesight. Elders accept this as their karam and do not imagine another life. Moneylenders, middlemen, police and politicians exploit them, and any attempt to organise is crushed.

Thus economic helplessness and blind acceptance of fate keep children trapped. Only education and courage, glimpsed in Mukesh’s dream of becoming a mechanic, can break the cycle.

questions.q: Compare and contrast the lives of Saheb and Mukesh. (120–150 words)
questions.answerHtml:
Saheb and Mukesh are both children of poverty whose childhood is stolen by work. Saheb, a ragpicker in Seemapuri, belongs to a migrant family from Dhaka; Mukesh is born into a family of bangle-makers in Firozabad. Neither goes to a proper school, and both live in squalid surroundings without basic facilities.

Yet they differ in outlook. Saheb is cheerful and curious, and wishes to study, but he drifts with circumstances. When he takes a job at a tea stall, he exchanges freedom for a fixed wage and becomes someone else’s servant. His dreams remain unspoken.

Mukesh, on the other hand, is determined to break free from his family’s traditional trade. He declares that he will become a motor mechanic and will walk to the garage however far it is. Saheb thus represents resignation to circumstances, while Mukesh represents the hope and willpower needed to escape the vicious circle.
